entries.title: Should Chicago continue to have delivery robots on city streets? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers whether Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/delivery-robots-chicago-food-coco-robotics" >should continue to have delivery robots on the city’s streets</a>. Here's what you said, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Yes, because they're less likely to kill a bystander than an Uber Eats driver staring at their phone behind the wheel."<br><i>— Collin Pearsall</i></p><p></p><p>"Chicago should not have delivery robots. These food delivery jobs are typically the types of jobs that our youth would have as they were finishing high school or during the summer. Our kids, and adults for that matter, could benefit from these jobs. It doesn't seem very smart to allow bots to take over the workforce, no matter how small it starts. Additionally, the property damage will only increase, and soon, more people will be injured too."</p><p><i>— Dee Crawford</i></p><p>"Delivery robots are part of our future. I support them. There have been very few glitches so far, and as far as I know, no one has been injured. The technology will continue to improve. Within a year or two, I doubt anyone will think twice about them."</p><p><i>— David Shiner</i></p><p>"Get these nuisances off our sidewalks."</p><p><i>— Bill Dahl</i></p><p>"Delivery robots and autonomous vehicles are just a way for tech companies to drain money out of Chicago and lay off workers. There is no benefit to the local economy."</p><p><i>— Mike McMains</i></p><p></p><p>"I would take more delivery robots on our sidewalks over the current situation. ... Our streets are routinely choked with double-parked delivery drivers. A drive along Lincoln Avenue between Webster and Fullerton any evening of the week is chaos."</p><p><i>— Tom Stroud</i></p><p>"Sure, any new technology has safety issues. My grandparents said their parents tried to stop the switchover to cars from horses. My grandparents envisioned giant planes crashing into schools and football stadiums. My parents thought microwaves would cook our brains."</p><p><i>— Linda Gies</i></p><p>"Yes, they’re cute."<br><i>— Valerie Morrow</i> </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/delivery-robots-chicago-food-coco-robotics" >What to know about Chicago’s delivery robots and the debate over them</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Storms possible as 'summer-like' conditions give way to much cooler temperatures Saturday in Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>"Summer-like" conditions bringing temperatures nearing 80 and a threat for severe storms Friday will give way to much cooler temperatures as the weekend progresses. </p><p>Highs were expected to reach 81 degrees Friday with a threat for large hail and damaging winds between 40 and 50 mph approaching by the evening, according to the National Weather Service. </p><p>"This could be our last summer-like day here for a little while," said Kevin Donofrio, a meteorologist with the weather service.</p><p>By Saturday, the high is expected be 30 degrees cooler than Friday, and by Saturday night temperatures could hover just above the freezing point, according to the weather service. A slight chance for rain was possible and wind gusts were expected to reach 30 mph. </p><p>Donofrio noted that a cold front moving through the central part of the United States is responsible for the approaching storm system and swing in temperature. </p><p>"Temperatures in the northern plains are in the 20s and 30s and that's pushing in our direction," Donofrio said. </p><p>Conditions are expected to be calm Sunday and Monday and highs in the 70s were expected to return by Tuesday. <br></p>

entries.title: Teen killed after crashing vehicle in Rolling Meadows industrial park
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old man was killed when police say he crashed his vehicle in a Rolling Meadows industrial park late Wednesday.</p><p>Rolling Meadows police said the crash happened just after 9:45 p.m. on the 3600 block of Industrial Avenue.</p><p>The driver was identified by the Cook County medical examiner’s office as Emilio D. Amaro. No hometown was given.</p><p>Police said Amaro was driving west on Euclid Avenue approaching Rohlwing Road with his vehicle’s headlights off when he passed a marked patrol car headed north on Rohlwing at Euclid.</p><p>For more on this story, please visit <a class="Link" href="https://www.dailyherald.com/20260417/news/teen-killed-after-crashing-vehicle-in-rolling-meadows-industrial-park/" target="_blank" >DailyHerald.com</a>.</p>

entries.title: CPS will be in session on May 1, but agreement with CTU encourages students to attend afternoon rally
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools will be in session for a full day on May 1, but it will also be an official civic day of action during which hundreds of students will be able to take a “field trip” to a massive pro-labor, anti-President Donald Trump rally.</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/12/chicago-teachers-union-plans-to-join-may-1-no-school-no-work-day-of-action-wants-classes-canceled" target="_blank" ><u>wanted the school district to cancel classes</u></a> so that staff and students could participate in May Day, also known as International Workers' Day.</p><p>But CPS CEO Macquline King pushed back, saying she wanted to keep schools in session. The disagreement kicked off a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/04/09/cps-will-be-open-may-1-during-protest-ceo-says-but-board-could-overrule-her/" target="_blank" ><u>firestorm of debate</u></a>.</p><p>On Thursday, they agreed to a compromise.</p><p>According to an agreement between CPS and the CTU, CPS will observe May 1, 2026 as a day of district-wide civic engagement.</p><p>To that end, 100 schools will be provided with buses and bag lunches so that students can attend an afternoon May Day rally. If the district can’t find enough buses, the city will pay for bus cards. </p><p>The district will also send out guidance to school leaders regarding the importance of civic engagement and suggest ways to involve students. </p><p>Also, the agreement says CPS cannot “retaliate against” staff who take the day off to participate in civic activities. </p><p>The agreement also releases 65 educators to go to Springfield to lobby for more state funds on May 13 and 27. Past CPS leaders have resisted releasing staff to do this kind of advocacy, even though the school district is in dire need of increased funding, largely due to the way the state funds schools.</p><p>The memo also designates May 1, 2028 as a teacher-directed professional day, meaning teachers could use it for civic action, and it creates a “May Day task force” between the district and CTU to “implement curriculum and school-based activities.”</p><p>Bridget Doherty Trebing, a teacher at Taft High School on the Northwest Side, said she thinks this compromise accomplishes CTU’s goal. She called the agreement “groundbreaking.”</p><p>“We have been asking all along to be in partnership with the district and it sounds like that is what has happened,” she said. “My students have been directly asking, when are more adults going to take a stand? They're paying attention to what's happening in the world. So this is a day that I think students are wanting to see.”</p><p>The CTU has been planning for a “no school, no work, no shopping” protest on May 1 for more than a year.</p><p>It’s long been a day to show support for labor unions and raise concerns about the government’s actions, but it's taken on new meaning this year as activists call for boycotting work to protest President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign and other policies enacted by his administration.</p><p>But for weeks, it was unclear who was calling the shots about May Day.</p><p>As recently as Thursday morning, Mayor Brandon Johnson <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/in-the-loop-with-sasha-ann-simons/2026/04/16/ask-the-mayor-april-2026-affordability-taxi-fares-new-zoning-chair-and-more" >said during an appearance on WBEZ</a> that he had directed his chief of staff and other city agencies to figure out logistics around the day. The CTU credited Johnson for helping come up with this compromise. </p><p>“If we’re going to transform our economies, if we’re gonna push for the ultra wealthy to pay their fair share in taxes, voices of working people, every day people have to rise up,” he told WBEZ.</p><p>The CTU thought King would go along with their plan after the school board took an informal vote in a closed session last week that showed the majority of members supported canceling school.</p><p>But even after that vote, King pushed back, saying she wanted an instructional day for students.</p><p>One Future Illinois, a super PAC that plans to be involved in the upcoming school board election, even commissioned a poll asking voters whether they thought CPS should be in session. Just over half opposed the idea of canceling school, while 40% said they were on board with school being canceled.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker also threw cold water on the idea of canceling classes for May Day when he was asked about it on Thursday.</p><p>“I think we need to make sure that our kids are getting every day of education that they deserve, and that parents demand,” Pritzker said. “Political operators trying to determine what the calendar should be for kids seems inappropriate.”</p>

Main</a></h5><p><b>No money</b>: Gregory Shell was once the right-hand man to Gangster Disciples boss Larry Hoover in a $100 million-a-year drug empire, according to federal authorities. Now, he says he’s flat broke. And he’s asking a judge to wipe out most of what’s left of his court fine. "It’s unfair," Shell said. "The interest is more than my original fine, which was $15,000."</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Shell and Hoover both were sentenced in the 1990s to life in prison for running a drug conspiracy. They were shipped to the nation’s toughest prison, the Colorado "supermax." Last year, they were sprung after winning presidential commutations of their federal convictions. But their legal troubles aren’t over. Hoover, 75, is still serving a state life sentence for murder and is asking Gov JB Pritzker for executive clemency.</p><p><b>Financial burden</b>: Shell, 68, is back at home on the South Side, and back in court, trying to get out of most of the remaining debt from his federal case. Former President Joe Biden, in one of his last moves in office, pardoned Shell in January 2025 and shaved $10,000 off his fine. Prosecutors say Shell still owes $1,461 in principal — plus a whopping $20,630 in interest on that — and argue he shouldn’t be let off the entries.title: Man sitting in car killed in South Deering shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man sitting in a car was killed in a shooting Friday morning in South Deering on the South Side. </p><p>The man, 44, was in the car around 10:50 a.m. in the 1600 block of East 95th Street when he was shot multiple times in the body, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Officer Krystal Rivera’s partner hid after fatally shooting her and failed to provide aid, new video shows
entries.summary: <p>Body camera footage released Friday shows that Chicago Police Officer Carlos Baker sat in a stairwell for more than 90 seconds after shooting his partner Krystal Rivera last summer, leaving her bleeding from a gunshot he initially said had been fired by someone else.</p><p>Videos show the officers chasing a man into an apartment building. Baker then booted open an apartment door and encountered a second man, who appears to aim a gun at the officers on videos released by the city’s Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>Baker turns, appears to trip over himself and fires the gunshot that hit Rivera, then runs up a stairwell and calls for help, the videos show. When Baker comes back down the stairs, he first steps over Rivera’s lifeless body before bringing her down the stairwell.</p><p>The video footage doesn’t show Baker rendering aid to Rivera.</p><div class="VideoEnhancement Enhancement" data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="video-de0000" name="video-de0000"></a> <div class="VideoEnhancement-player"><bsp-youtubeplayer data-video-player class="YouTubeVideoPlayer" data-player-id="fa4bb29e30dc24a6d9cccc91c1bef72e0" data-video-id="pC592whQ6Ww" data-video-title="Body-worn camera footage of Officer Carlos Baker from when his partner, Krystal Rivera, was killed" > <iframe id="YouTubeVideoPlayer-fa4bb29e30dc24a6d9cccc91c1bef72e0" allowfullscreen src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/pC592whQ6Ww?enablejsapi=1"></iframe> </bsp-youtubeplayer> </div> </div> <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/06/05/chicago-police-officer-shot-cpd-crime-shooting" target="_blank" >Rivera’s death</a> was the first fatal officer-on-officer shooting in Chicago in nearly 40 years, and the first since the widespread adoption of body-worn cameras in the 2010s.</p><p>COPA released only two videos related to Rivera’s death and didn’t say how many it withheld, a significant departure from past practice and apparently at odds with city policy requiring the release of videos and reports when an officer shoots someone.</p><p>In the shooting death of Adam Toledo, the agency released 23 body-worn camera video files. In the shooting death of Dexter Reed, the agency released 17 of those files, including video of officers who arrived after the shooting. In the most recent video release by COPA, from January, the agency released nine videos, including seven the agency tagged as occurring after the shooting. </p><h3><b>Rivera’s family says partner "Many officers would have ran down the … stairs possibly right away ... and subjecting themselves to then get shot.</p><p>“And then you'd have two shot officers on the staircase if the offenders were still in the apartment — which he had no idea that they had bailed at that point."</p><p>Authorities arrested and charged one man, accused of pointing a gun toward Baker once he was in the apartment, within a couple days of the shooting. The order prevented COPA from releasing videos within 60 days of the shooting, which is required by city ordinance.</p><p>The publisher of the Illinois Answers Project, the Chicago Sun-Times and other media organizations asked the judge to undo her secrecy order last summer. She declined, but an appeals court overturned her order in March as “an abuse of discretion.” COPA released videos and some files related to the shooting Friday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-710000" name="image-710000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c1cb0d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6881x3862+0+363/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2Fc8%2F35b017cc4eb5857b3744715ce2ca%2Fcopshot-060725-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2cb3574/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6881x3862+0+363/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2Fc8%2F35b017cc4eb5857b3744715ce2ca%2Fcopshot-060725-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/51db22e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6881x3862+0+363/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2Fc8%2F35b017cc4eb5857b3744715ce2ca%2Fcopshot-060725-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A building in the 8200 block of South Drexel Avenue on June 6, 2025 where Chicago Police Officer Krystal Rivera was fatally shot the night before. filled with guns and drugs.</p><p>Baker accrued five of those complaints as a probationary officer, when he could have been summarily fired because he had few union protections.</p><p>During that time, Baker was accused of flashing a gun at a woman he’d met online while she was on a date with another man at a North Side bar. as a stepping stone for promotions.</p><p>Between the two applications, Baker ran into more trouble.</p><p>He failed to activate his lights or sirens as he chased a stolen car in June 2024 that ultimately went flying into the air and wrecked six other vehicles, records show. Baker then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/02/19/chicago-police-department-krystal-rivera-carlos-baker-gresham-district-misconduct-discipline-investigation-cpd" target="_blank" >accidentally fired his Taser</a> while chasing the driver over a fence. He was docked two days of pay over the crash.</p><p>In between applications, he was also found to have been insubordinate and to have called his sergeant an expletive, records show. Baker had worked on the tactical team for a few months before shooting Rivera.</p><p>Each time Baker applied to the team, he had the backing of his district commander, Michael Tate, who worked under Supt. Larry Snelling in areas of the department where Snelling held top command positions earlier in his career.</p><p>Tate has declined to comment since the shooting, and the police department hasn’t answered questions about the shooting or Baker’s conduct. Tate was promoted late last year to street deputy, a high-ranking position responsible for responding to and commanding the scene at major events citywide.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/06/05/chicago-police-officer-shot-cpd-crime-shooting" target="_blank" >Chicago police officer was ‘unintentionally’ shot and killed by partner during Chatham foot pursuit</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/10/krystal-rivera-carlos-baker-chicago-police-department-wrongful-death-lawsuit" target="_blank" >Family of Chicago cop killed in botched chase sues Chicago Police Department and partner who shot her</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/06/27/krystal-rivera-carlos-baker-chicago-police-department-gresham-district-police-discipline-copa-civilian-office-police-accountability" target="_blank" >Chicago cop who inadvertently shot and killed his partner has a lengthy disciplinary record in a short career</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Marimar Martínez, a quien le disparó 5 veces un agente federal, testificará en audiencia en Washington
entries.summary: <p>Marimar Martínez, la mujer de Chicago que sobrevivió a cinco disparos de un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza (CBP), testificará ante el Comité de Seguridad Nacional en Washington, D.C. la próxima semana y el comité de los demócratas también están pidiendo que el subdirector de personal de la Casa Blanca, Stephen Miller, y “el zar de la frontera”, Tom Homan, comparezcan.</p><p>La comparecencia de Martínez, Miller y Homan es voluntaria en la audiencia del 22 de abril y llegó a solicitud de los demócratas de la minoría en el comité y el presidente republicano Andrew Garbarino, republicano por Nueva York, se aseguró de incluir algunas críticas a los demócratas en cartas enviadas el miércoles.</p><p>"El Comité no considera que esta solicitud sea de buena fe y se utilizará, en cambio, como un intento de politizar la seguridad nacional y engañar a la opinión pública estadounidense", escribió.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a50000" name="module-a50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El abogado de Martínez, Christopher Parente, confirmó el jueves su comparecencia en el segundo día de una audiencia destinada a discutir "los impactos perjudiciales del cierre del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) en los estadounidenses".</p><p>Los republicanos del comité están utilizando la audiencia para culpar a los demócratas por el cierre que ya ha durado 61 días.</p><p>Garbarino también criticó a la miembro del comité, la representante Delia Ramírez, demócrata por Illinois, en las cartas, escribiendo que Ramírez el 10 de febrero "se negó a permitir que los testigos respondieran a alguna pregunta", y declaró, "DHS no se puede reformar; debe ser desmantelado".</p><p>La audiencia del 22 de abril marcará la primera vez que Martínez testificará ante un comité oficial. Martínez compareció por primera vez ante el Congreso el 3 de febrero en un foro público organizado en respuesta a las muertes de dos residentes de Minnesota a manos de oficiales federales de inmigración, diciendo a los legisladores que quería que se responsabilizara a los agentes federales y escuchar una disculpa.</p><p>También dijo que quería que la administración de Trump reconociera <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatos" target="_blank" >que “no es una terrorista doméstica”</a>. Martínez también asistió a una audiencia del Comité Judicial del Senado el 3 de marzo, sentándose apenas cinco filas detrás de la entonces secretaria de Seguridad Nacional, Kristi Noem, mientras Noem era presionada por el senador estadounidense Richard Blumenthal, demócrata por Connecticut, a reconocer que el disparo a Martínez fue “incorrecto” durante una tensa audiencia.</p><p>A pesar de la cobertura exhaustiva del tiroteo de Martínez y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/11/21/desestiman-el-caso-contra-mujer-a-la-que-le-disparo-agente-de-la-patrulla-fronteriza-en-brighton-park" target="_blank" >los cargos de obstrucción a la justicia que fueron posteriormente desestimados</a> en su contra, Noem afirmó repetidamente que no conocía el caso.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/04/durante-audience-kristi-noem-dijo-no-conocer-a-marimar-martinez-la-mujer-de-chicago-a-la-que-un-agente-de-ice-le-disparo" target="_blank" >“Señor, no conozco la situación ni el caso”, dijo Noem</a>. “Lo investigaré para asegurarme de que todos los procedimientos se hayan seguido correctamente”.</p><p>Noem fue destituida de su cargo dos días después. Hubo murmullos de insatisfacción por parte del presidente Donald Trump tras dos días consecutivos de testimonios de Noem ante los comités del Senado y la Cámara.</p><p>Ramírez le dijo al Chicago Sun-Times que ve el testimonio de Martínez como una oportunidad para que los miembros republicanos del comité miren a un ciudadano estadounidense a la cara "y tengan que luchar con lo que hicieron para fallarle".</p><p>"Creo que es realmente importante que ella venga y confronte a las personas que son responsables de permitir lo que le sucedió, y que use su poder para poder hablar por la cantidad de personas que han sido baleadas, arrestadas, secuestradas y golpeadas por esta administración", dijo Ramírez. "Creo que también es importante para nosotros, y para personas como yo que representan a Chicago, darle más espacio y tiempo para poder aclarar tantos de los temas sobre los que estoy segura que van a intentar cuestionarla o, ya saben, mentir sobre lo que sucedió".</p><p>La congresista de Illinois calificó las críticas republicanas en las cartas del comité como "ridículas".</p><p>"La mayoría quiere encontrar cualquier excusa que puedan para no tener que ser confrontados por lo que están haciendo, pero también por lo que son cómplices", aseguró Ramírez. "No quieren ver a Stephen Miller y Tom Homan comparecer ante el comité. En algunos casos, es porque saben lo mal que están las cosas".</p><p>Los demócratas del comité han intentado citar a Miller y Homan, pero han sido rechazados por los miembros del partido republicano. Ramírez dijo que seguirán presionando por sus comparecencias y también están solicitando que Markwayne Mullins, el nuevo jefe de DHS, comparezca.</p><p>"Él debería venir ante nuestro comité para asegurarnos de que está tomando en serio estas reformas de políticas", aseguró Ramírez. "Sería inteligente por parte de Garbarino traerlo ante el comité para demostrarnos que él no es Kristi Noem, y que toma su trabajo y su juramento en serio, especialmente si quiere financiamiento".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Women's suffrage art that started in Chicago is growing across U.S.
entries.summary: <p>A series of women's suffrage murals that took root in Chicago is expanding across the United States. Three murals that pay tribute to the 1920 passage of the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote, have gone up in the Loop, and the murals have been so well-received that the organizers behind them are planning additional murals commemorating women’s suffrage in New York City and Portland, Oregon, as part of the National Suffrage Mural Series.</p><p>“People just don’t know that there was a time when women didn’t have the right to vote. They didn’t know that it took 70-plus years and multiple generations of women. They also don’t know that the effort was multiracial,” says mural series co-director Michelle Duster, a Chicago-based author, historian and the great-granddaughter of journalist and early civil rights leader Ida B. Wells.</p><p>Initially branded the Chicago Suffrage Mural Series, two of the three original murals, which were intended for a site near Columbia College Chicago, were blocked when a parking lot owner refused to rent the artists space to stage their paint and scaffolding. He called the murals “too political,” according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/11/15/22783199/speak-up-mural-womens-suffrage-columbia-college" target="_blank" >2021 Sun-Times story</a>. Two years later, the murals found their permanent home about a block away.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b30000" name="image-b30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/29ea3db/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4770x2677+0+251/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbe%2F4b6862f04ee69641f989b939b151%2Fmurals-suffrage-260419-08.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7d90c01/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4770x2677+0+251/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbe%2F4b6862f04ee69641f989b939b151%2Fmurals-suffrage-260419-08.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c2ba9a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4770x2677+0+251/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbe%2F4b6862f04ee69641f989b939b151%2Fmurals-suffrage-260419-08.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Two murals recognizing the women's suffrage movement appear on side of a building, one showing a yellow flower and one featuring the "... I'm speaking" phrase that Kamala Harris said during a vice presidential debate. Wabash Ave. often appear as backdrops on social media posts.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Given the current political climate, the message is especially important, say Duster and co-director Neysa Page-Lieberman, who previously served as executive director of Exhibitions and Performance at Columbia College and chief curator of the Wabash Arts Corridor.</p><p>“Our rights continue to be stripped away, and it’s accelerated in the past few years," Page-Lieberman says. "We can’t just rest on our laurels and think because we had this hard-fought, hard-won victory 100 years ago that we will always have that.”</p><p>The Chicago murals sit along the Wabash Arts Corridor in the Loop. They are made up of:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-b0024982-374f-11f1-9779-ab04fb0dfc67"><li>"On the Wings of Change" at 33 E. Ida B. Wells Drive by artist Jasmina<i> </i>Cazacu, who goes by the artist name Diosa. This portrait mural shows a teenage girl who seems to be dreaming of 10 Chicago suffragists, including Ida B. Wells. <a class="Link" href="https://library.colum.edu/archives/college-history/buildings/33-ida-b-wells-drive.php" target="_blank" >The building houses Columbia College offices, classrooms and the school’s radio station</a>.</li><li>"Speak Up!" at 623 S. Wabash Ave. by artist Dorian Sylvain. It features the popular quote that former Vice President Kamala Harris said in a debate with then-vice presidential candidate Mike Pence: “… I’m speaking.” <a class="Link" href="https://library.colum.edu/archives/college-history/buildings/623-south-wabash.php" target="_blank" >The building is owned by Columbia College and contains classrooms, offices, science labs, art studios and more</a>.</li><li>"Votes for Women,"<i> </i>also<i> </i>at 623 S. Wabash Ave. by artist AB Productions, includes a yellow rose, a symbol of suffragists, and commemorates 70 years of activism before women received the right to vote.</li></ul><div class="Enhancement" That was a way for me to make it more personal.”</p><p>Sylvain, of Hyde Park, said the "Speak Up" mural holds meaning for her after growing up in a politically involved home and witnessing the social changes of the '60s, '70s and '80s.</p><p>“As much as I can take for granted growing up in the time that I did, I also can really see how we are sliding backwards and it’s really frightening,” she says. For example, Sylvain witnessed Roe v. Wade pass, granting women the right to an abortion in all states, and then be overturned.</p><p>Now, the murals are regularly included on walking tours of the Wabash Arts Corridor, Duster says. She's met students from Roosevelt and Loyola universities and Columbia College who view them for different class assignments. Occasionally, the murals show up as backdrops on social media. </p><p>"You never know when it’s going to pop up," Duster says. If someone seeks a Chicago cityscape photo with a feminist angle, "they'll want that in the background."</p><p>In New York City, Little Village artist Sam Kirk is planning the next installment of women's suffrage murals.</p><p>The suffrage movement is “something that we’re living through in many ways right now,” she says. “I’m hoping that I’m able to remind people of that — how much work has been done and why we need to keep a lot of this work in place.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d00000" name="module-d00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Murals and Mosaics Newsletter</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div class="piano-sidebar-newsletter-murals-and-mosaics"></div> </div> </div></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Chicago’s murals and mosaics sidebar</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics" target="_blank" >Chicago’s murals & mosaics</a></h3>Part of a series on public art in the city and suburbs. <b>Know of a mural or mosaic? entries.title: Barbara Flynn Currie, 'trailblazer who opened doors for generations of women' dies
entries.summary: <p>After a vote in the Illinois House on a key part of then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s pension relief plan in 2016, Barbara Flynn Currie did something not often seen in these times of divided, dysfunctional government. She crossed the aisle and shook hands with the three Republican lawmakers who broke ranks with the GOP and voted to override Gov. Bruce Rauner’s veto of a measure deferring police and fire pension payments.</p><p>That was Currie, 85, who died Thursday. She not only represented her Hyde Park district in Springfield for 40 years — 20 as majority leader and the first woman to hold that role in the Illinois General Assembly — she was a tireless promoter of active, engaged, effective government.</p><p>"Last night we lost a giant," House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch, D-Hillside, posted on his Facebook page Friday. "Barbara Flynn Currie was more than a leader — she was a trailblazer who opened doors for generations of women in the Illinois House, many of whom continue her legacy today. ... She set the standard for what it means to serve with purpose. Her impact will be felt for generations."</p><p>Her district encompassed Hyde Park, Woodlawn, South Shore and Kenwood, and she was a vigorous proponent of liberal causes, such as prohibiting sexual harassment in the workplace, reforming school funding and offering all-day kindergarten. She spearheaded a compromise on welfare reform and helped extend state contracts to minority- and female-owned businesses.</p><p>In 2009, she chaired the special 21-member bipartisan committee that recommended the impeachment of Gov. Rod Blagojevich.</p><p>”We stand here today because of the perfidy of one man: Rod Blagojevich,” said Currie. “To overturn the results of an election is not something that should be undertaken lightly.”</p><p>Every member of the Illinois House and Senate, save one, voted to impeach.</p><p>With women making up a record 32% of state legislatures across the country, it might be difficult to remember the male world that Currie entered. When she was elected in 1978, fewer than 11% of Springfield lawmakers were women. When she announced her retirement in 2017, that figure was more than a third, and in 2025 the Illinois Legislature was 42% female. </p><p>Then-House Speaker Michael Madigan's decision to name her as majority leader in 1997 was unexpected: Downstate Democrats felt they had a hereditary right to the position, didn’t like the powerful post to pass to a Chicagoan, a woman, and perhaps worst of all, a liberal. Women across the spectrum saw it as a milestone.</p><p>”Republican women gave me flowers,” Currie later recalled. “Secretaries and staff in the Capitol were thrilled. One of my girlfriends nearly ran her car off the road. The depth of excitement was really quite thrilling.”</p><p>Still, some of Currie’s supporters looked askance at her playing ball with Madigan.</p><p>”To them, Currie was a sellout for taking the appointment from the hated machine politician Madigan,” Rich Miller of Capitol Fax wrote. “It never occurred to most of them that Currie’s new position would give their viewpoints an important new seat at the grown-ups table.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ad0000" name="image-ad0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a54186a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+1406/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2F7b%2F0451ff254f08aeb5aa1e1a7865f9%2Ffourth-cst-070514-10.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0aff75c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+1406/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2F7b%2F0451ff254f08aeb5aa1e1a7865f9%2Ffourth-cst-070514-10.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dc3cb7c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+1406/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2F7b%2F0451ff254f08aeb5aa1e1a7865f9%2Ffourth-cst-070514-10.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Barbara Flynn Currie at the annual Hyde Park Fourth of July parade in 2014. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Among the causes she promoted were gun control and abolishing the death penalty.</p><p>Barbara Flynn was born in LaCrosse, Wisconsin, the daughter of Francis and Elsie Flynn. When she was 7, her family moved to the South Side, where she attended St. Thomas the Apostle Catholic School and the University of Chicago Lab High School. Her mother was a schoolteacher, and her father taught social work at the University of Chicago, where she studied before dropping out to marry David Park Currie in 1960. Eventually she returned and received her bachelor’s degree in 1968 and master’s degree in 1973, both in political science.</p><p>She worked as vice president for the Chicago League of Women Voters from 1965 to 1969. Later, she taught government at DePaul University and was an assistant study director at the National Opinion Research Center.</p><p>Currie was elected to the Illinois General Assembly's 24th District in 1978; her district changed to the 26th District in 1983 and the 25th in 1993.</p><p>“Barbara Currie has tackled many, many complex issues with a keen intellect, fairness and balance,” Madigan said when she <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/9/15/18357519/house-powerhouse-barbara-flynn-currie-not-seeking-re-election" >announced her retirement </a>in 2017, opting to not seek reelection in 2018.</p><p>Her husband, a revered legal scholar and teacher, died in 2007.</p><p></p><p>Survivors include two children, Stephen and Margaret, and four grandchildren.</p>
